text:
This source gives a more precise naming system for the stages of a banana sucker as it develops from the corm, useful for judging exactly which offshoots on a clump are ready to dig for replanting:

- Peepers: the very first visible sign of a new sucker, just a small pointed nub breaking through the soil surface. Not yet usable for planting.
- Sword suckers: the preferred stage for digging and replanting. These have narrow, upright, sword-shaped leaves, a corm generally not wider than about 15cm across, and a sucker height (corm plus visible growth) of around 15-75cm. This is the stage described elsewhere (including in the newer MAFF manual) as the best planting material.
- Maiden suckers: a slightly earlier stage than the sword sucker, only 5-8 days past emergence, with just 1-2 leaves and an underdeveloped root system. Left in place, a maiden sucker will grow on quickly into a strong plant, but it is generally too immature to transplant successfully.
- Water suckers (broad-leaf suckers): suckers that develop from a weaker bud and have broad, less rigid leaves. These are generally discouraged as planting material because they tend to come from less vigorous growing points and produce weaker plants than sword suckers.

When selecting suckers for a new planting or for replacing a harvested mother plant, prioritize sword suckers over water suckers, and avoid digging suckers still at the peeper or maiden stage since they have not yet developed enough independent root mass to transplant reliably.
